tagline.text: Baguio's oldest heritage hotel, a wooden building from 1909

location.label: Location
location.text: Upper Session Road, Baguio City (Luneta Hill, right next to SM City Baguio)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–April dry season (book well ahead for the February Panagbenga festival)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–5,300 (per room per night, meals extra)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Overland from Manila Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL)

children.text: Casa Vallejo is a wooden building put up in 1909, in the American colonial period, as a dormitory for government employees; it became a hotel in 1923 and is known as the oldest hotel in Baguio. It stands on the hill above Session Road, within walking distance of the busy center, and you can look around the building and its restaurant even if you are not staying.

Casa Vallejo is a wooden building on Upper Session Road, on the slope of Luneta Hill in downtown Baguio, right beside the large SM City Baguio mall. Wikipedia says it was built in 1909 from wood, galvanized iron sheets and sawali (woven bamboo walls). Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap point to the same spot (about 16.41° N, 120.60° E), and it is generally described as the oldest hotel in the city.

It was not a hotel at first. While the Americans were developing Baguio as a summer capital, it housed employees of the Bureau of Public Works and was known as Dormitory 4. It is said to have held German prisoners of war in 1917, and in 1923 Salvador Vallejo leased the building and turned it into a hotel, which gave it its present name. In the 1940s it also served as a refugee center for British and Indian evacuees, and it came through the bombing of World War II. Sources differ somewhat on the building's uses and dates, so this article states only what several sources agree on.

On September 20, 2019, the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) unveiled a historical marker here. It is not a museum that sells tickets; it is still a working hotel, so visitors experience the building by staying overnight or by dining at the Hill Station restaurant inside. Creaking wooden stairs and worn corridors give you the atmosphere of a building more than a century old, which is its greatest charm. Remember that Baguio was planned in the early 1900s as the summer capital of the American colonial government, and this modest building becomes all the more meaningful as one of the few traces of the city's early days. Rather than expecting a glamorous hotel, come prepared to spend a night in a place where time has piled up.

It also helps to know about the dispute over the land under the building. In late 2013, descendants of an Ibaloi indigenous family petitioned the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) for a writ of possession, saying the land had been theirs since ancestral times. In January 2014, when eviction notices went out to tenants, artists, academics and citizens gathered in front of the hotel to protest. The NCIP chairperson issued a status quo order, so demolition was avoided, and petitions to have the building declared a heritage site continued among citizens. I could not confirm later legal developments, so check the hotel's official channels for its operating status before you visit.

The building is a colonial-era structure of wood, galvanized iron sheets and sawali. Seen from the road, its plain, long shape looks like an old school dormitory. Even if you are not staying, you can see the exterior and the marker from the street in front.

A marker unveiled by the National Historical Commission on September 20, 2019 confirms the building's official significance. Read the text on it to learn about the dormitory years and how the building became a hotel.

This restaurant inside the hotel is described as having the feel of an old dance hall and a menu that evokes old Baguio. Hotel guests eat breakfast here, and non-guests are said to be able to reserve dinner. Check the restaurant's Facebook page for the latest menu and hours.

The rooms have wooden floors and wooden walls, and there is no elevator. Some reviews say the hotel has been renovated and air-conditioned in recent years, but many describe the rooms and bathrooms as modest. Expect the sounds and dampness typical of an old building.

The hotel is at the top of Session Road, and walking downhill brings you to shops, cafes and restaurants. Many people also walk to Burnham Park and the night market area. It is a good base for seeing central Baguio without a car.

blocks.title: A building that gathered cultural spaces

children.text: Articles from 2012 to 2014 mention a bookstore selling Filipino authors, a space for independent films and a spa inside the building. I could not confirm whether they are still there, so check on site.

blocks.title: A starting point for a Baguio heritage walk

children.text: As one of the oldest buildings in the city, it makes a good start for a walk linking historic buildings and the cathedral. You can join the cathedral, Session Road and Burnham Park into a one-day route, and on the way you will feel the steep downtown slopes and the cool air of the highlands.
At Upper Session Road beside SM City Baguio, at the top of Session Road, look at the exterior of Casa Vallejo and its historical marker.
Ask at the front desk whether you may visit the lobby, and if so look around the corridors and stairs for the old atmosphere. Move quietly, as these are guest areas.
Have lunch or tea at Hill Station. Check the latest notices for the menu and opening hours.
Walk down Session Road toward Burnham Park, browsing shops and cafes. It is about
10–15 minutes
on foot.
The building is still a working hotel. It is not an attraction you can roam freely, so ask staff on site which areas you may visit.

items.title: One-night route
items.subtitle: A night in a heritage hotel

children.text: Check in and unpack. There is no elevator, so plan for carrying large bags up and down stairs.
Stroll along Session Road and Burnham Park. Baguio turns chilly after sunset, so bring a jacket.
Have dinner at Hill Station. It is safest to reserve before your stay.
The next morning, guests eat the hotel breakfast. It is described as included in the room rate, but confirm when booking.
Some reviews say street-facing rooms let in noise and that pedestrians can see in when the curtains are open. If you want a quiet room, ask when you book.
Buses such as Victory Liner and Genesis from Manila (Sampaloc, Cubao, EDSA and others) take about
5–7 hours
to reach Baguio. Some sources say expressway openings have shortened the trip.
Victory Liner regular air-conditioned buses were listed in March 2026 at about
from Sampaloc and Avenida and about
from Caloocan, with first-class seats costing more. Check the latest notices for fares and schedules.
Buses arrive at the city terminals in Baguio (Genesis, Victory Liner and others). From the terminal to the hotel, take a taxi or Grab.
In central Baguio you can use taxis, Grab and jeepneys, and the Session Road area can also be covered on foot.
SM City Baguio is right next door, so telling a taxi driver "Casa Vallejo next to SM" or "Upper Session Road" gets you there easily.
Walk uphill along Session Road from Burnham Park to reach the hotel. The slope is steady, so a taxi is easier if you have luggage.
If you bring a car, ask the hotel when you book whether parking is available and what it costs.
Baguio is cooler than the lowlands and pleasant all year, but the drier months of November to April are the most comfortable for walking around the building.
During the Panagbenga flower festival in February the whole city is crowded and rooms fill early, so book much further ahead.
In the rainy season of June to October, rain and mist give the old building more atmosphere, but roads are slippery and plans may change.

Casa Vallejo is itself the lodging. Room types have been described as Standard, Deluxe, Honeymoon and Family, and some rooms are on a floor below the lobby. Book through the hotel's official channels or a booking site; the official website is known as casavallejobaguio.com. Wikipedia lists 24 rooms, so check in advance for the peak season.

The main place to eat is Hill Station inside the hotel. One blogger recommended the steak and prawns and the callos (beef tripe stew), and guests are said to get breakfast. Outside the hotel there are many restaurants and cafes along Session Road, in SM City Baguio and around the Burnham Park night market. Baguio's strawberry sweets and souvenirs can also be bought near Session Road. If you are not staying, the easiest plan is to look at the exterior in the morning, have lunch at Hill Station and then walk down toward Session Road. The restaurant can be busy on peak-season weekends, so it helps to ask ahead.
The building is wooden, so sound carries. Move quietly in the corridors and rooms.
There is no elevator, so pack light or ask the staff for help with heavy luggage.
Street-facing rooms are busy and passersby may see in, so ask for a quiet room when you book.
Reserving dinner at Hill Station is safest. Ask the restaurant whether non-guests can dine.
Baguio nights are chilly. Bring a light jacket or cardigan.
Rooms tend to sell out during Panagbenga in February, so book months ahead.
Reviews of dampness and bedding in this old building are mixed. If something is wrong, say so at check-in.
If you like history, combine the exterior and marker with Session Road, the cathedral and Burnham Park on one walk.
Casa Vallejo is a working hotel, not a museum. Do not enter guest areas uninvited, and check its operating status and which areas are open to visitors before you go.
The building has been the subject of an ownership dispute. I could not confirm what happened afterwards, so check the hotel's official channels to see whether it is operating.
Room and extra fees differ greatly between booking sites, so compare the total before booking.
It is an old wooden building, so room condition and noise are not uniform.
Follow the hotel's policy on non-guests entering the building.
Bus fares and times change often. Check the latest notices.
The main street of central Baguio running downhill from the hotel; shops and restaurants begin within about
5 minutes
on foot.
A downtown park at the lower end of Session Road, with a lake, bike rentals and a night market.
A pink twin-towered church close to Session Road.
A former American military rest camp reached by taxi, good for strolls in the pine forest.
A downtown park known for its pine-lined path and horseback riding.
